items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Charlie Parker is mentioned by the interviewer and interviewee as a historical figure and influence ('rediscovering Charlie Parker', 'Charlie Parker knew how to do that'), but no personal interaction or direct professional relationship is described.

ctx.x: Would you even say that at that particular time that jazz was America’s popular music? Or did that particular form that the music found itself in, how did it communicate to an audience better than some of the songs today?

Well they could anticipate and memorize the melody and the lyrics, which is, as far as the period as far as I’m concerned, to the so-called originals that are being produced by everybody almost on the scene today. “I want to do my own things — I want to do my © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: He made him sound like he was talking about the same person. Them talking heads.

ctx.x: And from then on, every time he got into — well the talking heads kept going around. Isn’t that right Sonny? “Oh indubitably. He held the same intensity of emotions as for Charlie Parker with the exact same amount of platitudes as he did for Louis Armstrong.” He made him sound like he was talking about the same person. Them talking heads.

Well listen, as long as we’re on a few people I wanted to ask your maybe just reactions to a couple of names I’ll give to you. We already touched on Pee Wee Russell. Touch some more on Pee Wee Russell. What was it about him that was unique? Or maybe he wasn’t.
